Document Title: A Layout-Based Method for Analog Fault Injection in the Context of Functional Safety
Authors: R. Der Yeghiayan; P. Vilmercati; G. Storti Gajani; G. D’Alesio
Author Affiliations: STMicroelectronics, Cornaredo, Italy; STMicroelectronics, Cornaredo, Italy; Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria (DEIB), Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy; STMicroelectronics, Cornaredo, Italy
Abstract: Digital and analog circuits are fundamental components embedded across a wide range of applications, including but not limited to consumer electronics, automotive systems, aerospace technologies, medical instrumentation, and industrial automation. The critical role they play in ensuring the functionality and efficiency of modern technological systems introduces significant risks, as failures or defects can lead to catastrophic consequences. This work focuses on analog fault injection for automotive applications. ISO 26262 serves as the global standard for functional safety in automotive circuits, identifying fault injection as a fundamental approach to assess safety metrics and validate this category of circuits. Although fault injection is a well-known and widely adopted strategy in the digital domain, its usage is less widespread in analog circuits. The purpose of this work is to propose a layout-based method for analog circuits, where parasitic components in the post-layout extracted schematics are used as indicators to assign the likelihood of fault occurrence that may affect the functionality of circuits and impact the safety of the application. Moreover, the proposed approach leverages simulations to enable a quantitative assessment of the diagnostic coverage achieved by the implemented safety mechanisms. Although the results show a Diagnostic Coverage of 91.82%, which falls short of the assumed 99% by ISO 26262, the method provides valuable insights into identifying critical architecture or layout patterns that can be improved to achieve better safety metrics while maintaining electrical performance.
Author Keywords: Analog fault injection;analog circuit robustness;automotive safety;functional safety;ISO 26262;road vehicle safety

Document Title: Using Analog IJTAG to Measure ISO 26262 Metrics
Author Affiliations: Siemens EDA, Poznan, Poland; Siemens EDA, Ottawa, Canada
Abstract: The proposed P1687.2 analog extension to the widely used IEEE 1687 “IJTAG” standard for specifying digital IC tests and test access can greatly simplify writing production tests. This paper shows how the test language can support automated measurement of an analog circuit’s ISO 26262 functional safety (FuSa) metrics by an analog fault simulator. The Latent Fault Metric (LFM) is the percentage of faults in a safety mechanism (e.g., voltage monitor) that prevent detecting a second fault occurring in monitored circuit; it is challenging to measure because fault simulators typically simulate only one fault at a time. A two-step solution to this limitation is described that is safer and more efficient than simulating two faults at a time. The resulting design-for-test (DfT) and test methods are also suitable for production testing of the circuit. Simulated results for an automatically generated SPICE testbench for a commonly used circuit are provided - a bandgap voltage source supplying a voltage regulator monitored by two comparators connected to a second bandgap.
Author Keywords: IJTAG;design for test;functional safety;analog fault simulation

Publication Title: 2001 IEEE Autotestcon Proceedings. IEEE Systems Readiness Technology Conference. (Cat. No.01CH37237)
Abstract: A number of trends, including growing prime system complexity, the more widespread use of COTS equipment, an inclination to extended contractor support, and the increasing importance of global diagnostic coverage, all portend changes in the current system support paradigm. These changes will affect support acquisition, development, design and operational practice insofar as they relate to generic diagnostic functions and their realization using modern enabling technologies. Beneficial changes can be accelerated through the coordinated insertion of these technologies within the framework of a systems engineering process.

Document Title: ISO26262-compliant soft-error mitigation in register banks
Abstract: Temporary malfunction of ICs is often caused by Single Event Upsets (SEUs). That is why the automotive safety standard ISO 26262 demands measures to detect and mitigate a certain percentage of safety-critical SEUs. Different kinds of modules require different kinds of safety mechanisms. A frequently used module type is the Register Bank, which provides (quasi)static parameter settings to e.g. an analog block. A safety mechanism that detects and corrects SEU-caused failures in Register Banks is presented. Figures of Diagnostic Coverage and area overhead are shown for an automotive IC.
IEEE Terms: Registers;Safety;Integrated circuits;Decoding;Random access memory;Circuit faults;Automotive engineering

Document Title: Cyclisation of Safety Diagnoses: Influence on the Evaluation of Fault Metrics
Author Affiliations: Robert Bosch GmbH; University of Stuttgart
Abstract: This technical elaboration derives a new mathematical approach for Probabilistic Metric for random Hardware Failures (PMHF) calculation of intended functionalities that relate to cyclic safety measures with Diagnostic Coverage (DC). Thereby the probability density function of exponential failure distribution is adapted to the cyclic influence of safety diagnosis. All time dependent safety aspects of the system behavior are considered. That results in a piecewise density function, which is approximated for integration as a cumulative distribution function. This leads to a new definition of a cyclic DC rate and PMHF calculation. In addition to that, an appropriate FTA model will be described. Thereby, some current approaches of PMHF calculation are proven as incorrect for the target use case. Analysis and comparisons with state of the art will show the normative and engineering benefit of the concept. For example: a time discrete approach of the defined cyclic DC calculation method can be applied to predictive diagnostics and system state forecasting functions that are used in autonomous driving vehicles. This faces especially future vehicle applications. The new methodology will be illustrated with examples out of the area of vehicle powernet and safety diagnoses. The results of this investigation will be very valuable for safety engineers and auditors dealing with technical systems and implemented safety measures.ORGANIZATION OF THE ARTICLEStarting with the introduction of the general topic in section 1, the issues and objectives of the elaboration are given. The background information about vehicle powernet and basic information about safety measures are introduced as well as the related key points of the ISO 26262 safety validation process. Fundamental definitions of reliability engineering are stated in section 2. Based on this, the technical safety measure itself and its diagnostic functionality is introduced in section 3. The scope and underlying assumptions of the investigation are defined. In Section 4, the state-of-the-art approaches are introduced and discussed. After that, the novel approach for cyclic safety measures is elaborated and derived in detail which ends up in a FTA model assumption. In the last section 6, the results of all mentioned approaches are discussed and evaluated extensively using theoretical and graphical analyses. The accomplished engineering benefits of the novel approach are pointed out.
IEEE Terms: Measurement;ISO Standards;Random access memory;Reliability theory;Probability density function;Reliability engineering;Probabilistic logic

Authors: E. Barrera; M. Ruiz; A. Bustos; M. Afif; B. Radle; J. L. Fernández-Hernando; I. Prieto; R. Pedica; M. Barcala; J. C. Oller; R. Castro
Author Affiliations: Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain; Instrumentation and Applied Acoustic Research Group, Technical University of Madrid, Spain
Abstract: Interlocks are the instrumented functions of ITER that protect the machine against failures of the plant system components or incorrect machine operation. Regarding I&C, the Interlock Control System (ICS) ensures that no failure of the conventional ITER controls can lead to a serious damage of the machine integrity or availability. The ICS is in charge of the supervision and control of all the ITER components involved in the instrumented protection of the Tokamak and its auxiliary systems. It is constituted by the Central Interlock System (CIS), the different Plant Interlock Systems (PIS) and its networks. The ICS does not include the sensors and actuators of the plant systems but it is in charge of their control. The ITER interlock system shall be designed, built and operated according to the highest quality standards. The international standard IEC-61508 has been chosen as the reference. In both CIS and PIS cases two main architectures are used: a slow architecture, for those functions with response time requirements slower than 100ms (300 ms for central interlock functions), based on PLC technologies, and a fast architecture, based on FPGA technologies, for the functions with faster requirement times. The proposed design for fast PIS is based on the use of RIO (Reconfigurable Input/Output) technology from National Instruments (compactRIO platform). In order to provide a high integrity solution, a FMEDA (Failure Modes Effects and Diagnostics Analysis) has been conducted to analyze the components behavior. According to the output of the FMEDA a set of diagnostics has been defined and additional redundancy was added to the architecture to improve the integrity figures. The defined configuration has been called the “double-decker solution”, with two chassis running in parallel, communicated between them using a synchronous high speed serial line, and using redundant modules to implement the input and output measurement/excitations and redundant analog and digital modules to implement the diagnostics of these input/output modules. The integrity figures for the “double decker” solution are obtained from the classification of the failure rates, obtaining for the different configurations a SFF (safe failure fraction) of 85% and a FPH (Probability of dangerous Failure per Hour) of less than 1E-07. The FPGA design includes all the hardware to support the data acquisition from the input modules, the implementation of the diagnostics functionalities for analog and digital modules, the voting schema and the activation/deactivation of digital outputs. The platform includes an external test platform, also based on compactRIO technology, to perform the validation of the system and to register the performance of the different interlock functions implemented. The response times obtained for the TTL input to TTL output interlock function ranges from 5μs to 20μs; for the analog input to TTL output the response time is in the range of 41 μs to 90 μs, and for interlock functions using 24V digital input to 24V digital output, the time can rise up to 643 μs.
IEEE Terms: Field programmable gate arrays;Instruments;Time factors;Actuators;IEC Standards

Document Title: Failure Mechanisms Analysis for Integrated and Analog Position Sensors in Safety Relevant Automotive Use Cases
Author Affiliations: Department of Microelectronics, Faculty of Electronic Engineering, University of Niš, Niš, Serbia
Abstract: Modern vehicle architectures are requiring accurate positioning determination in variety of systems and system elements. Some of safety relevant examples of the position sensorics usage could include (but not be limited to) electromotor actuation, steering systems, braking & acceleration, shifting mechanisms and other systems. Connecting point of all these systems is a requirement for reliable intended functionality [1]. This aspect of reliability [2] requires careful structural top-to-bottom analysis of the possible failure mechanisms and outcomes (potential violation of safety goals [1] that may happen on a system level. This white paper will present some of the state-of-the-art Hall-effect based architectures that are available on the market, evaluate some key properties, analyze possible failure mechanisms, and propose some of the effective safety measures that may increase diagnostic coverage.

Document Title: A quantified safety analysis for Safety Fuzzy Logic Controller 1002 reliability block diagrams
Authors: M. Bsiss; A. Benaissa; H. B. Ibrahim
Author Affiliations: Department of computer science systems and telecommunications (LIST), Faculty of Science and Technology, Tangier, Morocco; Head of Department of computer science systems and telecommunications (LIST), Faculty of Science and Technology, Tangier, Morocco; Department of computer science systems and telecommunications (LIST), Faculty of Science and Technology, Tangier, Morocco
Publication Title: 2012 IEEE International Conference on Control System, Computing and Engineering
Abstract: This paper describes an analytical study to quantify the safety integrity of a Safety Fuzzy Logic Controller (SFLC) implemented in Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). In the area of the security of complex electronic systems, new Safety Standards as IEC 61508 occur and are designed to quantify the probability of dangerous failure (PFD) of a hardware failure of a system. The safety analyses addresses system architecture, hardware failure probability, diagnostic coverage factors and proof test interval. This quantification allows assignment of a Safety Integrity Level to a SFLC and will be taken, in consequence, of process hazard and risk analysis. This paper recalls the concepts of reliability block diagrams useful for calculating the probability of dangerous failure, including an explanation of the different parameters involved in the calculation.

Document Title: Thermal-Aware Signal Integrity and Fault-Propagation in Distributed Electrification Architectures for Intelligent Vehicles: A System-Level Safety and Reliability Analysis
Author Affiliations: ADAS Platform Hardware System Engineer and Independent Researcher, Ford Motor Company, Michigan, USA
Publication Title: 2026 IEEE 15th International Conference on Communication Systems and Network Technologies (CSNT)
Abstract: In this paper, the authors explore the interrelationship of thermal behavior, signal integrity, and functional safety in smart electric vehicle distributed electrification architectures. It investigates the role of skew and jitter caused by temperature variations and EMI drift on communication reliability of Battery Management Systems (BMS) and inverter networks based on CAN FD and daisy-chained SPI connections through secondary analysis of simulation and technical data. Thermal modeling indicates that increasing board temperature alters impedance and signal edge timing. The assessment of functional safety according to ISO 26262 Part 11 indicates that this kind of degradation increases the rate of hardware failures and expands the region of the diagnostic in safety-critical subsystems. Centralized, modular, and wireless BMS architectures were compared using a trade-off analysis between fault isolation, EMI resilience and control of latency. This work presents a system-level engineering analysis based on secondary simulation modeling and cross-reference of published FMEDA and reliability data; it does not claim recalculated quantitative safety metrics, but focuses on identifying thermal-EMI-signal-integrity interaction trends and their architectural safety implications. The combination of FMEDA data allowed confirming the relevance of early-stage modeling of the EMI-thermal interactions as a key to meeting the ASIL compliance. The paper arrives at the conclusion that shielding optimization, redundancy-based communication design, and predictive thermal management are useful in improving reliability, reducing the number of cascading faults, and maintaining deterministic operation. These results develop a thermal conscious design taking into account EMI suppression, signal resilience, and safety verification of next-generation distributed vehicle electrification systems. These findings support early architecture selection and interface partitioning for safety-critical EV networks.
Author Keywords: BMS;CAN FD;Daisy-Chained SPI;EMI;Functional Safety;Thermal Modeling;Fault Propagation;ISO 26262

Abstract: In this IP session, there will be 3 presentations focusing on functional testing and fault injection for automotive functional safety applications as well as a discussion on fault simulation and modeling for relevant analog test content. The 1st presentation will discuss verification solutions that accelerate fault injection for diagnostic coverage to meet ASIL requirements. The 2nd presentation discusses the use of focused random testing to achieve better functional coverage for automotive products. Document Title: Diagnostic Test Generation for Fault Localization in Printed Neuromorphic Circuits
Authors: T. Gheshlaghi; A. Studt; P. Pal; D. A. Moussa; M. Hefenbrock; M. Beigl; M. B. Tahoori
Author Affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT); Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT); Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT); Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT); Perspix.ai; Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT); Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT)
Publication Title: 2026 Design, Automation & Test in Europe Conference (DATE)
Abstract: Printed electronics (PE) enable lightweight, flexible, and low-cost devices for the Internet of Things (IoT) and wearable applications. Compared to conventional silicon-based electronics, PE trades peak performance for advantages in cost efficiency, mechanical flexibility, and large-area fabrication. However, its manufacturing processes remain unreliable and are prone to structural defects and variation due to inherent limited control in additive manufacturing. Printed neuromorphic circuits (pNCs) leverage the benefits of PE for on-demand analog edge computation in target applications but remain vulnerable to such defects. Diagnostic testing is therefore essential not only for detection but also for localizing faults to specific subcircuits and regions in the layout, a step critical for guiding yield improvement and reducing the cost of downstream inspection. We propose a diagnostic test pattern generation (DTPG) framework for fault localization in pNCs under black-box access. While ATPG is typically formulated as an optimization problem for fault detection, our approach extends this formulation by explicitly optimizing for fault distinguishability. On ten UCI datasets, the framework achieves up to 20.7% higher diagnostic coverage with a reduction of up to 3.6 times the number of undetectable subcircuits than detection-only test sets, while constraining the number of patterns to reduce storage overhead. These results demonstrate effective fault localization and establish a foundation for finer-grained, component-level diagnosis in future work.
Author Keywords: diagnostic test pattern generation;printed electronics;neuromorphic computing
